creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Found while an integrator agent drove five worker panes from a sixth (lore, 2026-09-04). Asked to size the five agent panes evenly, the agent had nothing to read: `muster window --json` gives `regions[]` with one weight per machine, and `panes[]` with tab, place and state, but nothing says how the tab's tree splits, which panes share a row or column, or how wide or tall each one is. The only recourse was to replay its own split order from memory (A right of the integrator, B below A, C right of A, D right of B, E right of C), infer that the top row must be 1/2, 1/4, 1/4, and issue two blind `pane resize --by` calls, then ask the person to look. A pane the person had opened in the same tab was invisible to that reasoning until `pane read` identified it.

Two asks. First, expose geometry: per pane, its share of width and height (or pixel size and origin), and enough of the tree to know neighbors - a `layout` field on the tab or a parent/split structure on each pane. That lets a script check the result of a resize instead of trusting it. Second, a verb for the common case so a script need not compute anything: `pane resize --equalize` over a tab, or over the row or column a pane sits in.

Related, minor: `pane resize` takes a share of the region, and after two blind calls nothing confirms where the divider landed. Done: an agent with no eyes can even out N panes in one command and verify from JSON that it happened.
title: 🧭 A script cannot see how a tab is laid out, so it cannot arrange one
